title: The Ansar weep
hook: after Hunayn the Ansar feel left out of the gifts, and he tells them: others go home with sheep and camels, and you with the messenger

segments.voice: Yesterday, the forgiven: Wahshi, Hind and Ikrimah came, and were received. Your line was: the door stayed open. Did you leave one open a crack? Day seven hundred ninety-two.

After the battle of Hunayn, there's a great deal to hand out. Flocks, herds, goods. And the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, gives generously, to leaders from Mecca and the tribes who have only just come over to Islam. The Ansar, the people of Medina who took him in when he had to leave Mecca, receive nothing from it. They notice. Some of the younger men talk. He gives to Quraysh, they say, while our swords still drip with their blood. Word reaches him. Today: the Ansar weep.
screen: `THE GIFTS OF HUNAYN.` → `NOTHING FOR THE ANSAR.` → `SOME OF THE YOUNG MEN TALK.`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari tells what he does. He doesn't send a message. He gathers the Ansar in one place, just them, and speaks to them directly. First he reminds them of what they've been through together. Didn't I find you astray, and Allah guided you through me? Divided, and Allah brought you together? In need, and Allah made you rich? And to each line they answer: Allah and His messenger are more generous. Then he turns it around. In Bukhari he tells them that if they wished, they could answer him back: you came to us like this, and like this. Ibn Ishaq's sirah fills it in: you came to us rejected, and we believed you; alone, and we helped you. He says their side of the story out loud for them. Then comes the line at the center of it all. Won't you be content, he asks, that people go home with sheep and camels, and you go home with the messenger of Allah? He tells them that if people took one valley and the Ansar took another, he would take the valley of the Ansar. In Ibn Ishaq's sirah, this is where they weep, until their beards are wet, and they say: we're content with the messenger of Allah as our share. One way to read it: the hurt wasn't really about camels. It was about whether they still mattered to him. So he didn't hand them more goods. He told them, plainly and in front of each other, what they meant to him. And the story's ending fits. After the conquest of Mecca, his own city, he went home to Medina with them, and stayed.
screen: `HE GATHERS THE ANSAR.` · `HE TELLS THEIR SIDE FOR THEM.` · `SHEEP AND CAMELS, OR THE MESSENGER.` · `THE VALLEY OF THE ANSAR.` · then, large: `YOU GO HOME WITH ME.`

segments.voice: The practice: tell someone what they mean to you. Rest your hands, and breathe out slowly. Bring to mind someone who has stood by you without much thanks. A parent, a friend, a coworker who covers for you. Ask yourself whether they might feel a little overlooked lately. Now, the way he did, say their side of it for them, quietly: you were there when I needed you. Then find the one plain sentence you'd want them to hear. Not a gift. A sentence. If you pray, you can ask Allah to bless them. The bell holds the time.
The Ansar weep. After Hunayn, the people of Medina felt left out of the gifts, and he told them that others go home with sheep and camels, and they go home with the messenger. Today's word.
Your line: you go home with me. Today, send that one plain sentence to the person you thought of, and tell them what they mean to you. Day seven hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the Prophet's speech to the Ansar after Hunayn from Sahih al-Bukhari and the sirah, and his words about the valley of the Ansar are quoted when people speak of the bond between him and the people of Medina.

fork.setup: you're the Prophet. the people who sheltered you feel left out of the gifts. what do you give them?
options: a larger share of the goods.
your words, and yourself: you go home with me.
fork.reveal: he gathered them and asked: won't you be content that others take sheep and camels, and you take the messenger home?

original.note: Arabic: 'the helpers', the name for the Muslims of Medina who took in the Prophet and those who emigrated with him.

trapdoor: what you thought: a quarrel over who got what.
what it means: the hurt was about belonging, so he answered with words about belonging, not more goods.
what a scholar hears: the speech in Bukhari's chapter on the campaign of Ta'if, with the weeping and 'content with him as our share' in Ibn Ishaq.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the Ansar's weeping after Hunayn)

notes: Editor: the young men's complaint now follows Bukhari (swords still dripping, gifts to Quraysh); Bukhari has only 'you could say, you came to us like this', so the fuller wording is credited to Ibn Ishaq; interpretation framed as one reading; 'the proof' softened.
Hadith numbers given from memory; confirm. The weeping and 'content with the messenger as our share' are from Ibn Ishaq; Bukhari's versions have the speech and the valley line. Confirm attribution.
'Some of the younger men talk' follows the Anas report in Bukhari; confirm.
The three 'didn't I find you...' lines and the 'you could answer me' turn are paraphrased and abridged; confirm order.
'He went home to Medina with them, and stayed' refers to his living and dying in Medina; confirm phrasing.
